In the United States, overall 5‑year relative survival for all cancers combined is roughly 68–69% (varies by cancer type, stage at diagnosis, age, and year). Individual cancers show wide variation: some rare cancers have only a few hundred cases per year, while the deadliest cancers can have very low 5‑year survival even if they are common.

1) Adrenocortical carcinoma — ≈200 new cases per year (US)
2) Thymoma (thymic epithelial tumors) — ≈400–500 new cases per year (US)
3) Penile cancer — ≈2,200 new cases per year (US)
4) Uveal (ocular) melanoma — ≈2,500 new cases per year (US)
5) Merkel cell carcinoma — ≈3,200 new cases per year (US)

Glioblastoma (primary malignant brain tumor) [~7% 5‑year survival]
Malignant mesothelioma [~10% 5‑year survival]
Esophageal cancer [~19% 5‑year survival]
Hepatocellular carcinoma (primary liver cancer) [~21% 5‑year survival]
Lung and bronchus cancer [~23% 5‑year survival]
